subject: 6 in 10 nannies don't make it. That's the pitch.
preview_text: A Bengaluru childcare startup that leads with who it turns away.
headline: 6 in 10 nannies don't make it. That's the pitch.
cover_alt: 6 in 10 nanny candidates don't clear Maasi's training, the company says.
lead_before_diagram: Maasi is a Bengaluru startup that trains, places and pays nannies. Aashu Manchali, Gargi Pandey and Reshov Roy launched it publicly on 20 October. A week later it raised a ₹6 Cr pre-seed round led by Better Capital, with Antler India.
The company says more than 4,000 parents joined its waitlist in the first five days. On-demand care starts at ₹199 an hour.
Think about what that ask really is. Not a card number. A parent is handing their child to someone they met last week. There's no purchase in a family that takes more trust.
So the interesting part isn't the round. It's how a brand-new company answers the three questions every parent asks before saying yes.
diagram_alt: Three parent questions mapped to Maasi's answers: Who is this person? Most candidates don't pass training. Will they be good with my child? Psychometric assessment and weeks of observation. Do parents like me use this? Built from Urban Parents Club, 8,000+ members.
lead_after_diagram: Look at where Maasi puts its effort. The training is free and led by preschool directors, nurses and former airline cabin crew trainers. The company says about six in ten candidates don't clear it. Those who do take a 16-point psychometric assessment and go through weeks of in-person observation. And Maasi didn't start from zero. It grew out of Urban Parents Club, a community of more than 8,000 Bengaluru parents.

Most brands hide their filter. They put a "verified" badge on the homepage and the details in an FAQ. Maasi leads with who it turns away, because a worried parent isn't reassured by how friendly you sound. They're reassured by how strict you are.

One honest caveat. These are a young company's own numbers, and its background checks run after a family picks a caregiver, not before. The real test is how many placements are still running in six months. But the way it earns trust is worth copying.
section_title: What this means for your brand
section_intro: Every category has a version of this. If your customer takes a real risk on you, the strongest trust signal you own is often the thing you say no to. Three things worth doing this week:

steps.title: Write down your filter.
steps.body: The customers, suppliers, hires or projects you turn away, and roughly how many. If you can't put a number on it, start counting.

steps.title: Make it something a customer can picture.
steps.body: "Verified" is a word anyone can use. "Trained by nurses and preschool directors" is a scene. Describe the process, not the badge.

steps.title: Move it to where the decision happens.
steps.body: Homepage, proposal, the first sales call. If your filter only lives in an FAQ, it's doing no work.

closer: Friendly gets you noticed. Strict gets you trusted.

short_takes.name: DriveU, Bengaluru
short_takes.body: DriveU sends a driver for your own car. Its FY26 profit after tax crossed ₹3.60 crore, up 109%, on over 2 million trips, and it says its NPS stayed above 60. Its last outside raise was in 2024, so growth is self-funded. When customers hand you their car keys, consistency is the marketing. Trip two million has to feel like trip one.

short_takes.name: ReplyAll
short_takes.body: A performance-wear brand founded in 2025 raised ₹9.7 crore, led by Sadev Ventures and Atom XVII. The number to notice: repeat customers bring in 40% of revenue, and three of its products have each sold out. The first sale proves your marketing works. The second proves the product kept its promise. Repeat rate is the most honest trust score a founder has, and no redesign can fake it.
